node.label: Joyce Appleby
node.date_label: Economic Thought and Ideology (1978) · Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984) · Telling the Truth about History, with Hunt and Jacob (1994) · Inheriting the Revolution (2000)
node.description: In Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984), Joyce Appleby argued that Jeffersonian Republicans envisioned a society of economically enterprising and politically equal individuals. Expanding commercial agriculture gave substance to that vision, making capitalism part of their challenge to inherited authority. Her Economic Thought and Ideology in Seventeenth-Century England (1978) had examined changing understandings of commerce and market forces. Wood’s 2000 review places her liberal Jefferson against the republican synthesis associated with Pocock, who disputed that characterization of his position. Wood praised the breadth of Inheriting the Revolution (2000) while questioning its chronology and explanation of change; Bushman, noting that its autobiographers were those with successful lives to write about, warned that readers might be drawn into the exuberance of liberal ideology and mistake it for the whole truth. With Lynn Hunt and Margaret Jacob, Appleby coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994). Chakrabarty’s 1997 engagement used that book to ask what kinds of past remain outside a discipline organized around shared rational standards of evidence. In “The Power of History” (1998), Appleby defended evidentiary constraint while urging historians to explain interpretation and revision to the public.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Economic Thought and Ideology in Seventeenth-Century England (1978); Capitalism and a New Social Order: The Republican Vision of the 1790s (1984); Liberalism and Republicanism in the Historical Imagination (1992); Telling the Truth about History, with Lynn Hunt and Margaret Jacob (1994); Inheriting the Revolution: The First Generation of Americans (2000); The Relentless Revolution: A History of Capitalism (2010).
node.scope_note: Selected primary web passages from “The Power of History” read, alongside publisher descriptions, Jacob’s biographical account, and selected Wood, Pocock, Chakrabarty, Cannadine and Bushman passages. Complete monographs, most cited underlying works, and the Harlan response are unread. Cannadine’s PDF text was readable; the attempted page-image check failed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Appleby and Hunt coauthored Telling the Truth about History (1994) with Margaret Jacob.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Norton author line names all three; AHA bibliography gives original 1994 publication. Norton’s displayed 1995 date is the paperback. Authorship only: the complete book is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gordon Wood's 2000 review credits Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984) with rescuing a liberal, commercially minded Jefferson from the 'republican synthesis' most associated with Pocock; Pocock replied (2000) that such a reading was compatible with his own argument.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wood, paragraphs beginning Several decades ago Appleby and In a series of important articles, explicitly identifies the 1984 book. Pocock’s 19 October letter rejects Wood’s dichotomy and says an entrepreneurial Jefferson could fit his argument. Mediated claim; neither monograph read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Liberal Jefferson and the republican synthesis (as framed by Wood; Pocock disputed)

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Early American Get-Up-and-Go” (2000), Wood praises the breadth of Appleby’s Inheriting the Revolution (2000) but questions its dating, account of the colonial order, and explanation of change through Jefferson’s election.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review paragraphs beginning Because Appleby often, Since Appleby does not describe, Moreover, Appleby never fully explains, and Still, despite these omissions. Selected review text read; Appleby’s monograph unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (1997), Chakrabarty uses Appleby, Hunt and Jacob’s Telling the Truth about History (1994) to question the epistemological limits of incorporating minority histories through shared rational rules of evidence.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Official AHA text, “Rationality in the Discourse of History,” paragraphs beginning The point about historical narratives and Nevertheless, and final “Subaltern Pasts and Disciplinary Limits” section. Calls the book “important” while extending the inquiry to exclusion. All three authors retain credit; book unread. Existing group edge_392 remains.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “What is History Now?” (published 2004), Cannadine recognizes a template for disciplinary essays in Appleby, Hunt and Jacob’s Telling the Truth about History (1994) and closes by endorsing Appleby’s “The Power of History” (1998).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Printed p. 50, section IV, notes 61–62: the template was encountered when the lecture was “nearly drafted”; n61 cites the 1995 book manifestation, p. 228, and n62 the 1998 address, p. 1. Retrospective recognition, not formative influence on the already drafted sections. Joint book unread; lecture delivery 2002 distinct from publication 2004.
proposed_edges.map_label: Cannadine acknowledges joint template and Appleby address

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Power of History” (1998), Appleby identifies Said’s Orientalism (1978) as a resource for historians’ scrutiny of Western representations of other peoples.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning Historians’ recent self-scrutiny and note 14 name Orientalism as “Particularly resonant.” Specific uptake; no full reading of Said asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Said as a resource for disciplinary self-scrutiny

proposed_edges.relationship: Capitalism and a New Social Order (1984) connects Jeffersonian political expectations to expanding commercial agriculture and a capitalist social vision.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: NYU description, final two argument paragraphs, explicitly links commercial agriculture, capitalism and the Jeffersonian movement. Publisher-mediated contribution; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Margaret Jacob’s AHA biography explains, Economic Thought and Ideology in Seventeenth-Century England (1978) reconstructs changing understandings of commerce and market forces by combining social practices with intellectual history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Jacob biography opening and paragraphs beginning Joyce’s first book and In her own life. Named substantive account of the method and subject; monograph unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Economic thought as intellectual and social history (1978)

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Power of History” (1998), Appleby argues that cultural mediation and historical revision can be explained publicly while material evidence continues to constrain historical claims.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Concluding paragraphs beginning We need to explain that historical knowledge, We could also make more salient, and History is powerful; phrase “materiality of historical evidence.” Primary web text read; print pagination uncollated. Adds a sole-authored intervention alongside the existing joint-book roster.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his response to critics (1999), Richard J. Evans disputed Joyce Appleby’s review “Does it really need defending?” (1997), arguing that she misrepresented In Defence of History (1997) as rejecting all postmodernism and defending an omniscient historian.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Evans’s reply, not Appleby’s original review or his book. His introduction at https://archives.history.ac.uk/history-in-focus/Whatishistory/evans.html dates the response November 1999 and lists Appleby’s review as TLS, 31 October 1997, p. 10. This records his objection without endorsing it.
proposed_edges.map_label: Evans disputes Appleby’s reading of historical objectivity

proposed_edges.relationship: In “More Pasts Than One” (1995), Eric Foner praised Telling the Truth about History (1994), coauthored by Joyce Appleby, Lynn Hunt and Margaret Jacob, but argued that its account underplayed the intellectual disruption of the 1960s and left historical truth insufficiently defined.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete publisher-hosted review. Its praise and reservations concern the joint book, not an argument attributed solely to Appleby. The book itself remains unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Foner questions the definition of historical truth

proposed_edges.relationship: The Relentless Revolution (2010) contributed to debate over capitalism’s origins by treating capitalism as a contingent cultural formation emerging in England; William Gallois’s 2010 review identifies this distinctive intervention while criticising its limited engagement with competing scholarship.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the review and Appleby’s response. Gallois explicitly assesses the book’s contribution and omissions; Appleby explains her distinction between earlier capitalist practices and capitalism as a culture. The book remains unread. No claim of priority or acceptance is made.
proposed_edges.map_label: Capitalism’s contingent English origins as a cultural formation
